prize_parts.citation: For the development of nanopore sensing, enabling electrical reading of single DNA and RNA molecules

statement.case_for: Nanopore sensing rests on one clear physical principle, the modulation of ionic current by a single molecule threading a molecular-scale channel, and it produced a capability nobody could foresee in 1990: portable, label-free, long-read single-molecule sequencing that also reads RNA and chemically modified bases directly. The chain of discovery can be stated simply to a broad audience: Deamer conceived driving a polynucleotide through a pore, Bayley engineered protein pores into stochastic sensors with single-base resolution, and Akeson showed that an enzyme ratchet can step DNA through the pore one nucleotide at a time, which is what made sequencing possible. It is mature (a decade of commercial use, independent validation, widespread clinical and field deployment) yet still advancing, so recognition is timely. It is also the only shortlisted candidate where a new measurement principle, rather than a new reagent or concept, defines the achievement.
statement.case_against: The founding claims are crowded. Branton and Kasianowicz demonstrated nucleic acid translocation through alpha-hemolysin, and a three-name citation that omits both is open to the charge of arbitrary cutting of the history. Part of the impact lands in genomics and could be seen as sequencing technology rather than chemistry. And the committee may reasonably prefer a candidate with a cleaner attribution, such as base editing, or one with larger present-day clinical impact.

responses.point: Base editing is a game-changer: a new class of tool, conceptually simple, with Liu as clear originator and Komor and Gaudelli as lead experimentalists on the two founding papers, already in clinical use and fitting Chemistry through protein evolution.
responses.response: I agree attribution is cleaner for B011 than for nanopores and I take that seriously as a genuine advantage; it is why I keep base editing as my first alternative. Where I differ is on what is new in kind. The adenine editor required real evolution chemistry, but the architecture is a deaminase fused to a Cas nickase, building on a platform the 2020 prize already honoured. Nanopore sequencing introduces a new transduction principle. Johan, I would like to hear whether you think a Liu prize can be explained as a distinct chemical discovery rather than a CRISPR extension, because that is the argument I would need to be persuaded by.

responses.point: For base editing Peter asks what is new chemically, noting that much of the novelty is biochemical engineering of an existing CRISPR system, and he regards it as possibly premature compared with more established methods.
responses.response: Peter's question is the right one and it narrows my doubts about B011 rather than removing them; I share his reading that the deaminase chemistry itself is not new. I would apply the same test to nanopores and answer it differently: the new element is a single-molecule electrical readout of a polymer with monomer resolution, which I would call analytical chemistry in its own right. His own first choice, Pd-catalysed amination (B058), is mature and attractive on attribution, but it extends the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and I would want him to say what the committee gains beyond that precedent.

responses.point: Targeted protein degradation is a new modality in which designed small molecules recruit an E3 ligase and remove the target, reaching proteins thought undruggable, with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli as a plausible trio and approval still pending.
responses.response: I find the principle compelling and the design logic genuinely chemical, which is why B038 is my second alternative. My reservation is that the concept is split into two distinct stories: PROTACs (Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli) and thalidomide-type glues (Handa, Ito), and a trio cannot honour both. Daniel's trio also tacitly leaves the cereblon work out. Without an approved degrader the maturity argument rests on trials still under way. I would ask whether the committee prefers a single combined citation or a later separate prize for glues.

responses.point: Andrei ranks B038 first for turning the ubiquitin-proteasome machinery into programmable chemistry, and for nanopores acknowledges that a three-name list omits Branton and Kasianowicz.
responses.response: I appreciate Andrei acknowledging the same allocation problem in B003 that I see. My answer is that a Nobel citation must name the conceptual origin, the enabling engineering and the demonstration of sequencing, and Deamer, Bayley and Akeson cover those three roles; Branton shares the early concept with Deamer, and I would welcome a view from him or Peter Brzezinski on whether the Branton-Deamer priority is separable. I disagree gently that B038 timing is plausible rather than premature: without an approved degrader the clinical validation is thinner than the decade of nanopore sequencing.

uncertainties: Whether the Branton and Kasianowicz claims for the first nucleic acid translocation experiments can be separated from Deamer's conception well enough to defend a three-name list.
Whether the committee regards nanopore sequencing as chemistry or as genomics technology.
Whether base editing can be framed as a distinct chemical advance rather than an extension of the 2020 CRISPR prize.
How the committee weighs mature, cleanly attributable work against fast-moving clinical fields.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the credited candidates for B003, B011 or B038 is at Lund University or otherwise connected to me, though my own nanophysics work (nanowires, molecular motors) is topically adjacent to nanopore sensing.
